newsitem.title: UK: British PM heads for subcontinent ahead of election.
newsitem.headline: British PM heads for subcontinent ahead of election.

text.p: British Prime Minister John Major leaves for India, Pakistan and Bangladesh on Wednesday in his last big foreign trip before an election.

With polls giving the opposition Labour party a lead of around 20 points, and with four months at the most to go to the election, some ruling Conservative party members of parliament have questioned the wisdom of such a journey.

But aides to Major, who is taking one of the largest groups of businessmen to accompany him on a foreign trip, say the growing importance of India as a trade partner means the visit makes good commercial sense.
"This is about cementing relationships and opening doors for the future," said one senior aide who will be travelling with Major.
British trade with India has almost doubled in the last four years, to around 3.5 billion pounds ($5.93 billion) in 1996.

Trade Secretary Ian Lang, who is travelling with the party to concentrate on trade issues when Major takes time out for talks with the region's leaders, said before the trip: "India and Pakistan represent two of our key markets.
"On my last visit to India last January, I announced a target for two-way trade of five billion pounds by the year 2000."

The emphasis on trade is highlighted by the list of businessmen travelling, which includes British Telecom chairman Iain Vallance, British Airways chief executive Robert Ayling and Adair Turner, director general of the top employers' group, the Confederation of British Industry.
But the trip, which begins in Calcutta on Thursday and ends in Lahore next Tuesday, will not be devoted entirely to trade and commerce.
Major is scheduled to meet Indian Prime Minister Deve Gowda, Bangladesh prime minister Sheikh Hasina and Pakistan's caretaker premier, Meraj Khalid, as well as opposition leaders.
Major, a keen sports fan, is also expected to snatch an hour or two in India to watch the Lancashire cricket side take on a local team.

He is also scheduled to travel up the Khyber Pass, the legendary strategic gateway between Afghanistan and the Indian subcontinent which has a key historical importance for the British army regiments who defended it.
But Major, who aides say has no other foreign trips plannedd, is unlikely to escape British politics entirely.

With a 23-strong corps of reporters and cameramen from British newspapers, television and radio travelling with him, any statement or slip will be immediately interpreted in the light of the bitter unofficial election campaign which is already underway. ($1=.5904 Pound)
